title: Visible Speech
target_users: Readers of visible speech, including deaf people (to verify)
procedure: Readers learned to read speech from the sound spectrograph (details to verify).
limits: Readers were taught phonetic principles.
finding: Bell Labs' programme to let deaf people 'see' speech with the sound spectrograph. Historical background; readers were taught phonetic rules, so it does not meet the training rule.

title: Perception of visual transforms of speech stimuli: A preliminary experiment
compared: With vs. without a visual display; display size, aspect ratio, familiarity with spectrograms
procedure: Identify words in noise.
limits: Known only from a catalogue summary.
finding: Adding a visual display of speech improved word intelligibility in noise. Varied display size, aspect ratio and familiarity. [Ours: one of the few studies on display parameters we have found.]
source_note: Link is a catalogue summary, not the paper. Participants' training level and display timing to verify.

title: Learning to identify visual displays of speech: A first report
compared: Trained talker vs. new male, female and synthetic talkers
procedure: Whole-word identification training, then generalization tests.
limits: Meeting abstract; same study as Greene et al. (1984).
finding: Early report of the 1984 study. The authors describe generalization to new male, female and synthetic talkers as 'relatively high'.
source_note: Link is a catalogue summary, not the paper; original to find.

title: Identification of speech spectrograms: Comparisons of naive and trained observers
venue: Research on Speech Perception, Progress Report 9, Indiana University
compared: Naive observers after ~15 h whole-word training vs. observers who had taken MIT's spectrogram-reading course
procedure: Identify phonetic segments in unfamiliar words.
limits: Figures from a secondary summary.
finding: On unfamiliar words, naive observers identified 33% of phonetic segments and observers trained in spectrogram reading 40%.
source_note: Figures from a secondary summary of a JASA meeting abstract; that abstract and this report are assumed to be the same study.

title: Recognition of speech spectrograms
post_hoc_explanation: Observers relied on 'salient visual correlates of many phonetic features' rather than formal phonetic knowledge (abstract).
compared: Trained words vs. new tokens, new male and female talkers, synthetic speech
procedure: ~20 h of training to identify 50 words from spectrograms, then generalization tests; verbal protocols.
limits: [Ours] Closed set of 50 words; few talkers.
finding: Over 95% correct on the 50 trained words. New tokens of the same talker 91%, new male and female talkers 76%, synthetic speech 48%. Observers relied on visual correlates of phonetic features.

title: Difficulty in learning to read speech spectrograms: The role of visual segmentation
venue: Technical report LRDC/PITT/IMP-1, Univ. of Pittsburgh
post_hoc_explanation: A 'within-object search bias': cues inside one visual object are found more easily; a salient enough cue can override it (full text).
compared: Cue type (several cues vs. one; within one visual object vs. across two), instructions, cue salience
procedure: Learn to classify synthetic pseudo-spectrograms of CVC syllables by trial and feedback until a criterion; a separate group circled the regions they found salient.
limits: Pseudo-spectrograms, not real speech; weak instruction manipulation (author).
measures: Trials to criterion; circling of salient regions
finding: 9/10 learned /b/–/p/, 6/10 /t/–/k/, only 2/10 /d/–/g/, whose cue sits in the next vowel's formants. A separate group circled 'important parts': vowel formants 98%, consonant formants 76%. Proposes a within-object search bias.

title: How well can children recognize speech features in spectrograms? Comparisons by age and hearing status
target_users: Children with and without hearing loss
population: 60 children aged 6–11, half with hearing loss
compared: Age group; hearing status; contrast type (formant vs. consonant manner)
procedure: Brief familiarization with spectrographic cues, then pick which of three spectrograms matches a model.
limits: [Ours] Matching, not identification.
finding: After brief familiarization, children picked the matching spectrogram out of three above chance. Formant contrasts were easier than consonant-manner contrasts; hearing status made no difference.

title: Classification of large acoustic datasets using machine learning and crowdsourcing: Application to whale calls
compared: Crowd similarity judgments vs. machine-learning clustering
procedure: Whale FM volunteers heard and saw whale calls and picked similar ones.
limits: [Ours] Audio and spectrogram together, not vision alone.
finding: Volunteers matched whale calls using spectrograms together with audio. Their judgments recovered geographic and subspecies groupings, less accurately than machine learning.
source_note: Background: the spectrogram was a tool for crowdsourced labelling, not the object of study; volunteers also heard the audio, and the display was neither varied nor evaluated.

authors: Song, Zhang, Peng, Mohaghegh, Wandt & Rhodin
title: AudioViewer: Learning to visualize sounds
target_users: DHH people (intended); tested with hearing participants (to verify)
compared: High-res faces (CelebA) vs. digits (MNIST) vs. mel-spectrogram vs. a lip-sync (talking-head) method
procedure: Study I: match and group sounds from their visualizations. Study II: 9 participants learned four words over 16 rounds.
finding: Study I overall accuracy: faces 86.4%, digits 79.7%, mel-spectrogram 66.2%, lip-sync faces 47.7%. Study II final accuracy: AudioViewer 87.0% vs. mel-spectrogram 57.8%.
source_note: Presented as sensory substitution for DHH people ("helping hearing impaired persons to see what they can not hear"); participants appear to be hearing (to verify). Numbers from the arXiv full text; check against the WACV version.

title: Teaching new vowel sounds using real-time spectral displays
compared: None; change across trials
procedure: Produce an unfamiliar vowel while matching a real-time spectral display to a template.
limits: Template showed only part of the spectrum (authors).
finding: Participants learned an unfamiliar vowel by matching a real-time spectral display to a template, with marked change within the first 100 attempts, although the template showed only part of the spectrum.

title: Comparison of two visual display devices in speech-training of deaf adolescents
compared: Visible Speech Translator (scrolling spectrogram) vs. Lucia Spectrum Indicator
procedure: Speech training on the word 'see'.
limits: Known only from a catalogue summary.
finding: The Visible Speech Translator (scrolling spectrogram) and the Lucia Spectrum Indicator gave the same training results.
source_note: Link is a catalogue summary, not the paper; original to find.

title: Evaluation of a spectrographic display as a speech training aid for the deaf
compared: Practice with a real-time spectrogram vs. training by teachers
procedure: Children practised production with the display, including on their own.
limits: Known only from a catalogue summary.
finding: Practice with a real-time spectrogram was as effective as training by teachers, and even the youngest children could use it on their own.
source_note: Link is a catalogue summary, not the paper; original to find.

title: Real-time spectrographic displays in vowel production training with children who have profound hearing loss
compared: Baseline vs. spectrographic training
procedure: Vowel production training with a real-time spectrogram; probes on untrained words.
finding: Vowel accuracy improved once spectrographic training started, with some transfer to untrained words.

title: A comparison of speech training methods with deaf adolescents: Spectrographic versus noninstrumental instruction
compared: Spectrographic vs. noninstrumental instruction
procedure: Speech production training with both methods.
limits: Design type to verify.
finding: Both spectrographic and traditional instruction improved production quickly; two participants generalized better with the spectrographic display.

title: Real-time feedback in the singing studio: an innovatory action-research project using new voice technology
procedure: Action research with singing teachers and students using real-time displays.
finding: VOXed project: real-time displays in singing lessons. Which displays were used (pitch, spectrogram, others) is to verify.

title: Are real-time displays of benefit in the singing studio? An exploratory study
limits: Not yet read.
finding: Exploratory study of real-time displays in singing lessons. Design and displays not yet read.
source_note: Found by title search; authors, year and link to verify.

title: Effects of two-month vocal exercising with and without spectral biofeedback on student actors' speaking voice
compared: Two months of vocal exercise with vs. without spectral biofeedback
procedure: Speaking-voice exercises.
limits: Only the title is verified.
finding: Only the title is confirmed. Reported elsewhere: voice quality improved in both groups, a little more on one measure with feedback, and watching the display may encourage excess vocal effort.

title: Differential effects of visual-acoustic biofeedback intervention for residual speech errors
sound_properties: formants (F3 relative to F2) with target
compared: Biofeedback (LPC spectrum + template) vs. traditional articulatory treatment; order counterbalanced
procedure: 10 sessions of each treatment (crossover).
finding: No overall difference from traditional treatment, but a condition × order interaction: biofeedback looked more effective in the first phase. [Ours: the display may help most while a new target is being acquired.]

title: Efficacy of visual–acoustic biofeedback intervention for residual rhotic errors: A single-subject randomization study
sound_properties: formants (F3 relative to F2) with target
compared: Biofeedback vs. traditional sessions in randomized alternation
procedure: 20 sessions over 10 weeks.
limits: Children whose errors earlier treatment had not fixed.
finding: Four of seven responded to treatment; for three, gains within a session were larger with biofeedback than with verbal cues.

authors: McAllister Byun, Campbell, Carey, Liang, Park & Svirsky
title: Enhancing intervention for residual rhotic errors via app-delivered biofeedback: A case study
sound_properties: formants (F3 relative to F2) with target
compared: Accuracy with the display vs. probes without it
procedure: App-delivered LPC biofeedback with an adjustable F3 target.
limits: One participant.
measures: Accuracy in treatment; probes without feedback
finding: staRt app (LPC curve + adjustable F3 target). Accuracy during treatment rose from 1% to 73%, but the gain did not carry over to words produced without the display.

authors: McAllister, Preston, Benway, Hill, Lara, Leece, Liang & Hitchcock
title: Rhotic acquisition is more rapid in biofeedback than motor-based treatment for residual speech sound disorder
sound_properties: formants (F3 relative to F2) with target
compared: Biofeedback (visual-acoustic or ultrasound) vs. motor-based treatment
procedure: Treatment sessions; primary outcome over the first three sessions.
limits: Preregistered.
finding: Biofeedback produced faster progress than motor-based treatment. No significant difference between the acoustic display and the ultrasound display of the tongue.

title: The effect of concurrent visual feedback on adult singing accuracy
compared: Concurrent visual feedback vs. none; acquisition and retention (per Zhang 2026)
procedure: Sing target pitches.
limits: Not yet read.
finding: Concurrent pitch feedback; Zhang (2026) reports better accuracy during training and a drop once feedback was removed. Not yet read.
source_note: Pitch display: included only if criterion 2 is widened to non-spectral acoustic displays.

title: The effect of visual and auditory feedback on adult poor-pitch remediation
compared: Visual vs. auditory feedback
procedure: Remediation training for poor-pitch singers.
limits: Not yet read.
finding: Visual vs. auditory feedback for poor-pitch singers. Not yet read.

title: Real-time visual feedback for pitch matching
compared: Real-time visual pitch feedback vs. comparison condition(s) (to verify)
procedure: Pitch-matching training, then transfer tests.
finding: A real-time pitch display improved pitch matching, and the gain was retained in transfer tests.
source_note: Zhang (2026) cites this DOI under different authors (García-García & Tejada).

title: Real-time visual feedback without knowledge of results (cited in Blanco et al., 2021)
compared: Real-time visual feedback with vs. without knowledge of results
procedure: Pitch matching.
limits: Known only through Blanco et al. (2021).
finding: Real-time visual feedback without knowledge of results did not improve pitch matching.

title: Can you see what I hear? The design and evaluation of a peripheral sound display for the deaf
target_task: Stay aware of sounds at work
sound_properties: full spectrum vs. location and loudness
compared: Spectrograph vs. positional ripples
procedure: Deaf participants identified sounds with each display and reported preference.
finding: Compared a spectrograph with positional ripples. Participants preferred the display without pitch that showed location, and found it easier to monitor.

title: Evaluating non-speech sound visualizations for the deaf
sound_properties: full spectrum vs. recognized sound class
compared: Several visualizations, from spectrograph to icons
procedure: Interviews and evaluation of design alternatives with deaf participants.
finding: Icon-only was liked most; spectrograms were called distracting and noisy. Some participants wanted to interact with the spectrogram by producing sounds, and it drew attention well when a loud sound occurred.
source_note: Details from Xuehua's reading of the full text.

title: Head-mounted display visualizations to support sound awareness for the deaf and hard of hearing
target_task: Locate speakers and sounds in conversation
compared: Design alternatives for showing sound on a head-mounted display
procedure: Formative study with design probes, then a prototype test.
finding: Head-mounted display designs centred on where a sound comes from.

title: SPECTRA: Personalizable sound recognition for DHH users through interactive machine learning
compared: Representations for inspecting sounds (spectrogram, waveform, others)
procedure: Train a personal sound recognizer; rate representations; interviews.
finding: Spectrograms rated 5.1/7 vs. waveforms 6.7/7. 'I don't identify things in my life really based on frequency as much as I do based on loudness.'

authors: de Lacerda Pataca, Watkins, Peiris, Lee & Huenerfauth
title: Visualization of speech prosody and emotion in captions
target_task: Understand emphasis and emotion in captions
sound_properties: prosody and emotion, shown in typography
compared: Caption designs with and without prosody or emotion
procedure: Watch captioned videos; answer questions about emphasis and emotion; rate legibility and preference.
finding: Captions carrying emotion conveyed emphasis and emotional content best, with only a modest cost in legibility. Visualizes extracted features, not spectrograms.

title: Enhancing musical experience for the hearing-impaired using visual and haptic displays
sound_properties: note data from MIDI (which parameters: to verify)
compared: Within subjects: music only / + visuals / + Haptic Chair / + both; later synchronized vs. asynchronous gesture videos
procedure: Three 1-minute MIDI pieces per condition; 3-week follow-up with 6 participants.
limits: The authors note that musical experience is more than flow. [Ours: 1-minute trials; participants knew the study's purpose; no measure of what the visuals conveyed; reported df suggest ratings were treated as independent rather than repeated measures, to check.]
measures: Flow State Scale (6 items); preference ranking; observable flow indicators; USE satisfaction questionnaire
finding: The Haptic Chair dominated; visuals beat music alone, but no one chose visuals alone. Abstract particles had limited effect; synchronized human gestures beat asynchronous ones.
source_note: Visuals are driven by MIDI note data, not audio: included under the criterion-3 exception for displays designed for and evaluated with DHH users.

title: Formalizing knowledge used in spectrogram reading: Acoustic and perceptual evidence from stops
compared: Readers vs. listeners
procedure: Identify stop consonants from spectrograms of 299 talkers.
finding: Readers identified stop consonants from 299 talkers at 73–82%, about 10 points below listeners, using explicit rules.

title: Spectrogram reading and expert methods for acoustic-phonetic speech signal decoding
compared: Isolated words vs. connected speech
procedure: Expert decoding of speech from spectrograms.
finding: About 87% of segments correct for isolated words, 83% for connected speech; accuracy 'practically does not depend on speaker's voice quality'.

title: Creating access to music through visualization
finding: Music visualizations for DHH audiences. Original not yet located.
source_note: Cited in Xuehua's earlier notes; venue, design and link to verify.

authors: Aslan, Griggio, Pohl, Merritt & van Berkel
title: Speejis: Enhancing user experience of mobile voice messaging with automatic visual speech emotion cues
target_task: Notice the emotional tone of voice messages
sound_properties: emotion (paralinguistic processing and continuous emotion models)
compared: Voice messaging with vs. without speejis
procedure: Use voice messaging in both conditions; rate experience.
finding: Significant differences in attractiveness and stimulation, and a clear preference for messaging with speejis.
source_note: Fits the revised criteria (hearing users, others' voice) but none of the current three criteria, so it has no lane on the timeline. Peer-reviewed version to check.
